extracted.subtask_description: A practical, step-by-step guide for writers creating historical fiction novels, covering concept selection, research, structure, plotting, character development, drafting, revising, and professional editing. Geared toward turning a historically grounded idea into a finished, publishable manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop your story concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose how history will function in your story: fictionalised accurate retelling, a true story with creative license, real events as backdrop for mostly fictional characters, or using a true story merely as inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide lists four approaches: (1) 'Tell a fictionalised (but accurate) version of a true story' (including biographical historical fiction), (2) 'Tell a true story with some creative license' — allowable to draw on gaps/subtext but be honest in your historical note, (3) 'Use real events as the backdrop for your mostly fictional story' — core story largely invented though real figures may appear, (4) 'Use a true story as the inspiration for your fictional story' — base fictional characters on real people only with caution. Anti-patterns: 'blatantly fabricate and falsify key elements of history.' Legal note: 'avoid basing your characters on people who are still living (for obvious legal reasons).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Start thorough research (primary and secondary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Figure out what you need to know and compile relevant resources, aiming for a balance of primary and secondary sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary sources give authentic flavour and voices; secondary sources provide wider perspective. Take plenty of notes and record provenance (who wrote a source and why). Cross-reference sources because 'sources sometimes contain errors.' If your period is very old and sources are sparse, fill gaps plausibly but document choices in your historical note. Research is ongoing: 'Research never really stops, even when you’ve started writing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Strike a balance between accuracy and creative license
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for historical accuracy and authenticity while accepting limited creative license where necessary, and be transparent about liberties taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect an absorbing story and immersion in a period that 'feels true.' Accurately depict everyday life and the wider political backdrop. Most readers 'will tolerate a little creative license as long as you justify it in your historical note,' but 'filling your novel with numerous egregious falsehoods about easily verifiable facts is likely to get you into trouble.' Use the historical note to explain gaps and how you filled them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduce authentic speech and social conventions; avoid anachronism
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray how people spoke and behaved in the period; avoid modern slang or attitudes that break immersion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide warns: 'There’s little worse in a historical novel than a character speaking in modern slang or acting as if they’re in the 21st century.' Pay attention to social conventions and modes of speech appropriate to the era. Use primary sources to shape authentic voices, but avoid stilted pastiche — authenticity should support story and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick your structure (plot structure, narrative structure, viewpoint, tense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make deliberate decisions about plot architecture, temporal/narrative layout, point of view, and tense early in planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choices to consider: (1) plot structure — e.g. the three-act structure (beginning ~25%, middle ~50%, end ~25%); (2) narrative structure — single chronological timeline vs multiple timelines, single vs multiple points of view; (3) viewpoint — first person, third-person limited, third-person omniscient; (4) tense — past vs present (past feels 'historical'; present feels 'in the moment' but may jar). The guide notes there is 'no right or wrong answer' and each option has risks and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a compelling plot (story question, conflict, stakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your plot contains a clear story question, driving conflict, and meaningful stakes that make outcomes matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'story question' is 'the central question your reader wants to know the answer to' and is resolved at the end. Conflict is 'the clash between your main characters and the forces and obstacles' and is the main driving force. Stakes are 'the consequences of success or failure' — ask 'what's the worst that could happen if your protagonist fails' and 'what's the best if they succeed.' The gap between best and worst gives the story its importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop rich, complex characters (aims & motivations, internal conflict, character growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create characters with clear aims and motivations, layered internal conflicts, and believable growth over the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should have aims that propel them and motivations that make those aims feel real; without aims they feel directionless. Internal conflict adds emotional power and drives choices; external conflict keeps plot momentum. Ensure characters evolve: 'If they don’t [grow], they’ll come across as too rigid and predictable.' Growth can resolve internal conflict or show overcoming fears/flaws by the story’s end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline progressively (one-sentence to one-page summaries; include resolution and profiles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft a tiered outline starting small (one-sentence) and expanding to detailed summaries and character profiles to organize plot and historical detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested progression: one-sentence summary capturing story question and main character, then one-paragraph including antagonist and key events, then one-page expanding the paragraph. If using three-act, highlight key act elements (e.g., act endings). Include character profiles (main and secondary) with backgrounds, aims, motivations, external/internal conflicts, and sections for building a historically authentic setting. The guide provides a novel outline template tailored to historical fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep researching while writing and document sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Continue research during drafting and keep meticulous notes about where information comes from and why you chose interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide emphasizes research 'never really stops' and suggests recording where 'vital bits of information come from.' Check provenance and cross-reference because 'the likely purpose of a source affects how we should read it.' If you invent details when evidence is lacking, document how you filled gaps for the historical note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start drafting with a sustainable routine and appropriate tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin writing once planning and research are sufficient; develop a writing rhythm and use tools that support your process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't have to write daily, but 'it is important to find a rhythm.' Set a schedule and stick to it where possible. Tool recommendations: Microsoft Word, Scrivener (author-focused), Dragon (dictation), Grammarly and ProWritingAid (grammar/style checking). Use group coaching or accountability for support, feedback, and discipline. Anti-pattern: delaying writing because research feels incomplete — 'it’s part of the same process.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise with distance and a plan (take time off, read whole, make an editing plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: After completing a first draft, step away (recommendation: six weeks), then read through without editing to identify issues and create a targeted revision plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended process: take ~six weeks off, 'read the whole thing through without any editing the first time; just make notes as you go along,' then review notes and make a short editing plan. Work chapter-by-chapter to make corrections, additions, deletions, and track 'knock-on effects' where changes ripple elsewhere. Expect multiple revision rounds; aim for a complete second draft before external editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire professional editing appropriate to the stage (content edit, copy-edit, proofread)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage professional editors when the manuscript is ready: a content edit for story-craft and structure, followed by copy-editing/proofreading for self-publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A content editor provides expertise in story-craft and spot weaknesses you may miss due to proximity. For self-publishing, 'it’s best to get a professional copy-edit and proofread once you’ve settled the big-picture elements.' Editors are more than a fresh pair of eyes: they help 'turn your story into the best possible version of itself' before submissions or publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about historical liberties in a historical note
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain to readers what you invented, interpreted, or altered from the historical record, and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where you take creative license or fill gaps, 'be honest with your reader in your historical note.' Use this note to justify liberties and explain how gaps were filled so readers and historians understand your choices. This transparency reduces reader backlash over inaccuracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid egregious factual errors and respect verifiable facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not populate the novel with easily verifiable falsehoods; prioritize getting verifiable facts correct to maintain credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide cautions that while small liberties are tolerated, 'filling your novel with numerous egregious falsehoods about easily verifiable facts is likely to get you into trouble.' Use cross-referencing and provenance checks to avoid repeating errors found in sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate research resources and specialist tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage online archives, primary sources, images, maps, language tools, and specialist blogs to build authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide points readers to its '50+ top online research resources' which include online archives with thousands of primary sources, image/video/audio resources, maps, language tools, and specialist blogs. Use such resources to reproduce authentic setting details and voices.
